rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. An intermediate temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

Keep the gradient unchanged and raise temperature to test selectivity of the sole critical early pair. The higher temperature should also shorten retention, preserving room below the 10-minute time-penalty threshold.

Injection 2 reached the maximum CRF; shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. Keep temperature and endpoints fixed to isolate the effect of gradient steepness on the critical early pair.

Use a slope between injections 2 and 3 to recover the early pair’s resolution while retaining some time savings. The last peak’s estimated elution fraction was about 0.58, so an endpoint of 0.85 leaves ample elution strength.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving injection 4’s slope to test whether retention can be shortened without losing full resolution. The early pair is the main risk; injection 4 remains a maximum-score fallback.

Test the low-temperature selectivity regime with the faster gradient, since the critical pair may reverse order and separate better on cooling. This explores an alternative route to full resolution while retaining the maximum-score methods already found.

Return to the successful high-temperature regime and test a slope just steeper than injection 4, targeting full resolution with a shorter programmed gradient. The last peak may elute briefly into the final hold, so this run also tests how tightly the endpoint can be trimmed.

Test whether a modest temperature increase separates the late cluster seen at 25 C while preserving the favorable early-pair selectivity. The steeper gradient probes a potentially faster alternative to the fully resolved 60 C methods.

Test whether a substantially steeper gradient breaks up the late three-peak cluster at 25 C through slope-dependent selectivity. Comparing with injection 6 will reveal whether this low-temperature branch can yield a faster fully resolved method.

The late cluster barely responded to slope at 25 C, so return to 30 C and test a higher starting organic fraction. This probes whether shifting the gradient window can shorten retention while improving the critical late-pair selectivity; injection 7 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Raise temperature one step from injection 10 to test whether the late cluster reaches full resolution before the early pair becomes limiting. Keeping the gradient fixed isolates this selectivity tradeoff and should shorten the last peak’s retention.

Reduce gradient steepness by 25% to improve the early pair that limits injection 11, while retaining the temperature that resolved the late cluster. The endpoint remains above the last peak’s estimated elution fraction, with room to lengthen retention before the time penalty begins.

Refine the fastest fully resolved branch with a slightly shallower slope than injection 7 and an endpoint high enough to keep the last peak inside the gradient. This targets a little more resolution margin while retaining a last-peak time near seven minutes.

Pair the higher starting fraction tested in injection 5 with a shallower gradient to recover its early-pair resolution. This tests whether a shifted window can maintain maximum CRF with retention close to the fastest fully resolved methods.

Shift injection 12’s window upward while keeping its slope fixed to test starting-composition selectivity of the early pair. This should shorten retention and determine whether the intermediate-temperature branch can achieve full resolution.

Probe just beyond injection 7’s successful gradient steepness, with a higher endpoint to avoid a final hold. This tests the boundary for a faster maximum-score method; the early pair may fall slightly below R = 1.5.

The speed boundary is now bracketed by injections 7 and 16. Test a shallower gradient to increase resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes, seeking a less marginal maximum-score method.

Raise the starting fraction relative to injection 17 while retaining a similar slope, aiming to shorten retention and improve the second close pair’s separation. The early pair should retain more resolution margin than in injection 14, potentially giving another maximum-score method.

Steepen injection 18’s gradient to shorten retention while targeting early-pair resolution just above 1.5. This slope lies close to the successful boundary established by injection 14 and should preserve the maximum CRF.

Use a slope between injections 2 and 17, with a trimmed endpoint that should still accommodate the last peak. This targets greater resolution margin than the fastest method while keeping all peaks below the 10-minute penalty threshold.

Trim injection 2’s endpoint and gradient duration while preserving its successful slope. This should retain full resolution and a last peak near 7.5 minutes, with less programmed gradient time and a stronger final wash than injection 7.

Refine near injection 17 with a slightly shallower slope, aiming to balance the two closest pairs near R = 2 while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. Injection 7 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-score method.

Shift the starting fraction upward and flatten the gradient relative to injection 22 to seek balanced resolution margins for both close pairs. The last peak is expected near 8.5 minutes, preserving maximum CRF if all pairs remain resolved.

Shorten retention relative to injection 23 using the lower starting fraction and a steeper gradient, targeting full resolution with more margin than injection 7. Nearby successful slopes suggest a last peak around 7.9 minutes and a minimum resolution around 1.8.

Shorten injection 23’s gradient to eight minutes, using a slope slightly shallower than the fully resolved injection 14. This should preserve maximum CRF with a last peak near 7.3 minutes; injection 7 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method.
